The **French Bulldog**, [French](French_language "French language"): **Bouledogue Français**, is a French [breed](Dog_breed "Dog breed") of [companion dog](Companion_dog "Companion dog") or [toy dog](Toy_dog "Toy dog"). It appeared in Paris in the mid-nineteenth century, apparently the result of [cross-breeding](Cross-breeding "Cross-breeding") of [Toy Bulldogs](Toy_Bulldog "Toy Bulldog") imported from England and local Parisian [ratters](Ratter_(dog) "Ratter (dog)").[[4]](French_Bulldog#cite_note-Le_bouledogue_Français,_Ses_origines-4)

It is commonly kept as a pet, and is among the most frequently registered dogs in a number of countries including Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

## History

From the beginning of the nineteenth century [bulldogs](Bulldog "Bulldog") were bred in the United Kingdom for purposes other than traditional [blood sports](Blood_sports "Blood sports") such as bull-baiting, which were banned in 1835.[[5]](French_Bulldog#cite_note-coile-5): 5 By the middle of the century there were miniature bulldogs, often weighing some 7–11 kg (15–24 lb), though some weighed considerably less.[[5]](French_Bulldog#cite_note-coile-5): 6

At the same time, [lace](Lace "Lace") workers from <Nottingham> who were displaced by the [Industrial Revolution](Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution") began to settle in <Normandy>, France.[[6]](French_Bulldog#cite_note-leighton-6): 58 They brought a variety of dogs with them, including Toy Bulldogs.[[7]](French_Bulldog#cite_note-Get_to_Know_the_French_Bulldog-7) The dogs became popular in France and a trade in imported small Bulldogs was created, with breeders in England sending over Bulldogs that they considered to be too small, or with faults such as ears that stood up. By 1860, there were few Toy Bulldogs left in England, such was their popularity in France, and due to the exploits of specialist dog exporters.[[5]](French_Bulldog#cite_note-coile-5): 6

The small Bulldog type gradually became thought of as a breed, and received a name, the Bouledogue Francais.[[5]](French_Bulldog#cite_note-coile-5): 6 This Francization of the English name is also a contraction of the words *boule* ('ball') and *dogue* ('mastiff'). The dogs were highly fashionable and were sought after by society ladies and Parisian prostitutes alike, as well as creatives such as artists, writers, and fashion designers.[[5]](French_Bulldog#cite_note-coile-5): 6 The artists [Edgar Degas](Edgar_Degas "Edgar Degas") and [Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec](Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec "Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec") are thought to have French Bulldogs in their paintings.[[8]](French_Bulldog#cite_note-:2-8) However, records were not kept of the breed's development as it diverged further away from its original Bulldog roots. As it changed, terrier stock had been brought in to develop traits such as the breed's long straight ears.[[5]](French_Bulldog#cite_note-coile-5): 6

The **dachshund** ([UK](British_English "British English"): /ˈdækshʊnd, -ənd, -hʊnt/ *DAKS-huund, -⁠ənd, -⁠huunt* or [US](American_English "American English"): /ˈdɑːkshʊnt, -hʊnd, -ənt/ *DAHKS-huunt, -⁠huund, -⁠ənt*;[[1]](Dachshund#cite_note-1)[[2]](Dachshund#cite_note-2)[[3]](Dachshund#cite_note-3)[[4]](Dachshund#cite_note-4) German: "[badger](Badger "Badger") dog"), also known as the **wiener dog**, **badger dog**, **doxie**, and **sausage dog**, is a short-legged, long-bodied, [hound](Hound "Hound")-type [dog breed](Dog_breed "Dog breed"). The dog may be smooth-haired, wire-haired, or long-haired. Coloration varies.

The dachshund was bred to [scent](Macrosmatic "Macrosmatic"), [chase](Hunting "Hunting"), and flush out badgers and other [burrow](Burrow "Burrow")-dwelling animals. The miniature dachshund was bred to [hunt](Hunt "Hunt") small animals such as [rabbits](Rabbit "Rabbit").[[5]](Dachshund#cite_note-5)

According to the [American Kennel Club](American_Kennel_Club "American Kennel Club"), the dachshund was ranked 9th in popularity among dog breeds in the United States in 2022.[[6]](Dachshund#cite_note-6)

## Etymology

Look up ***[Dachshund](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Dachshund "wiktionary:Dachshund")*** in Wiktionary, the free dictionary.

The name *dachshund* is of German [origin](Word_origin "Word origin"), and means "badger dog," from *[Dachs](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Dachs#German "wikt:Dachs")* ("badger") and *[Hund](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Hund#German "wikt:Hund")* ("hound, dog"). The German word is pronounced [ˈdaks.hʊnt] [](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/8/8d/De-Dachshund.ogg/De-Dachshund.ogg.mp3)ⓘ. The pronunciation varies in English: variations of the first and second [syllables](Syllable "Syllable") include /ˈdɑːks-/, /ˈdæks-/ and /-hʊnt/, /-hʊnd/, /-ənd/. It may be incorrectly pronounced as /ˈdæʃ-/*hound* by some English speakers.[[7]](Dachshund#cite_note-7)[[8]](Dachshund#cite_note-8) Although *Dachshund* is a German word, in modern German family dogs are more commonly known by the short name *Dackel*. Working dogs are, less commonly known as *Teckel*.[[9]](Dachshund#cite_note-9)

Because of their long, narrow build, they are often nicknamed wiener or sausage dog.[[10]](Dachshund#cite_note-10)

The **Pug** is a [breed of dog](Breed_of_dog "Breed of dog") originally from China, with physically distinctive features of a wrinkly, short-muzzled face, and curled tail. The breed has a fine, glossy coat that comes in a variety of colors, most often [fawn](Fawn_(color) "Fawn (color)") (light brown) or [black](Black "Black"), and a compact, square body with well developed and thick muscles all over the body.

Pugs were brought from China to Europe in the sixteenth century and were popularized in Western Europe by the [House of Orange](House_of_Orange-Nassau "House of Orange-Nassau") of the Netherlands, and the [House of Stuart](House_of_Stuart "House of Stuart").[[2]](Pug#cite_note-Pugs_in_public-2) In the United Kingdom, in the nineteenth century, [Queen Victoria](Queen_Victoria "Queen Victoria") developed a passion for pugs which she passed on to other members of the Royal Family.

Pugs are known for being sociable and gentle [companion dogs](Companion_dog "Companion dog").[[3]](Pug#cite_note-Morn-3) The [American Kennel Club](American_Kennel_Club "American Kennel Club") describes the breed's personality as "even-tempered and charming".[[4]](Pug#cite_note-AKC_Breed_Standard-4) Pugs remain popular into the twenty-first century, with some famous celebrity owners. Pugs are susceptible to various health issues due to their bred traits.[[5]](Pug#cite_note-5)

## Description

### Physical characteristics

While the pugs that are depicted in eighteenth century prints tend to be long and lean,[[2]](Pug#cite_note-Pugs_in_public-2) modern breed preferences are for a square [cobby](Cobby_dog "Cobby dog") body, a compact form, a deep chest, and well-developed muscle.[[4]](Pug#cite_note-AKC_Breed_Standard-4) Their smooth and glossy coats can be fawn, apricot fawn, silver fawn, or black.[[4]](Pug#cite_note-AKC_Breed_Standard-4)[[6]](Pug#cite_note-6) The markings are clearly defined and there is a trace of a black line extending from the occiput to the tail.[[4]](Pug#cite_note-AKC_Breed_Standard-4) The tail normally curls tightly over the hip.[[2]](Pug#cite_note-Pugs_in_public-2)

Pugs have two distinct shapes for their ears, "rose" and "button". "Rose" ears are smaller than the standard style of "button" ears, and are folded with the front edge against the side of the head. Breeding preference goes to "button" style ears.[[7]](Pug#cite_note-7)

Pugs' legs are strong, straight, of moderate length and are set well under. Their shoulders are moderately laid back. Their ankles are strong, their feet are small, their toes are well split-up, and their nails are black.[[4]](Pug#cite_note-AKC_Breed_Standard-4) The lower teeth normally protrude further than their upper, resulting in an under-bite.[[1]](Pug#cite_note-AKC_History-1)

### Temperament

This breed is often described by the Latin phrase *multum in parvo*, or "much in little" or "a lot of dog in a small space", alluding to the pug's remarkable and charming personality, despite its small size.[[1]](Pug#cite_note-AKC_History-1) Pugs are strong-willed but rarely aggressive, and are suitable for families with children. Shih Tzus are known for their short snouts and large round eyes, as well as their long coat, floppy ears, and short and stout posture. They are well known for their playful personality and their calm and friendly temperament.[[1]](Shih_Tzu#cite_note-1)

They can adapt well to different situations. Due to their highly independent nature, they are not considered as a very obedient breed.[[2]](Shih_Tzu#cite_note-2)

## Description

The Shih Tzu is a sturdy dog with a small [muzzle](Snout#Dogs "Snout") and normally has large dark brown eyes. The Chinese have described their head shapes as "owl head" and "lion head", and their mouth as "frog mouths".[[3]](Shih_Tzu#cite_note-Juliette._2007-3) They have a soft and long double coat that will tangle and mat easily if not brushed at least every 2 or 3 days. A Shih Tzu should stand no more than 26.7 cm (10 1⁄2") at the [withers](Withers#Dogs "Withers") and with an ideal weight of 4.0 to 7.5kg (9 to 17 lb). Their floppy ears are covered with long [fur](Fur "Fur"), and their heavily fur-covered [tail](Tail "Tail") is carried curled over the back. The coat may be of any colour, though white and with blazes of grey are frequently seen. A very noticeable feature is the [underbite](Underbite "Underbite"), which is required in the [breed standard](Breed_standard "Breed standard").[[4]](Shih_Tzu#cite_note-FCIstandard-4)

Because of their long coat and fast-growing hair, regular grooming is necessary, which may be expensive. The traditional long silky coat, which tends to reach the floor, requires daily brushing to avoid tangles. The coat can be clipped short to simplify care, but still requires frequent brushing. For showing, the coat must be left in its natural state, though trimming for neatness around the feet and anus is allowed. The shorter cut is typically called a "puppy cut"[[5]](Shih_Tzu#cite_note-5) or a "teddy bear cut" when the puppy cut is accompanied by a fuller, rounder face, resembling a stuffed animal.

The **beagle** is a [breed](Dog_breed "Dog breed") of small [scent hound](Scent_hound "Scent hound"), similar in appearance to the much larger [foxhound](Foxhound "Foxhound"). The beagle was developed primarily for [hunting](Tracking_(hunting) "Tracking (hunting)") [hare](Hare "Hare"), known as [beagling](Beagling "Beagling"). Possessing a great sense of smell and superior tracking instincts, the beagle is the primary breed used as a [detection dog](Detection_dog "Detection dog") for prohibited agricultural imports and foodstuffs in [quarantine](Quarantine "Quarantine") around the world. The beagle is a popular [pet](Companion_dog "Companion dog") due to its size, good temper, and a lack of [inherited health problems](Dog_health#Genetic_diseases "Dog health").

The modern breed was developed in Great Britain around the 1830s from several breeds, including the [Talbot Hound](Talbot_(dog) "Talbot (dog)"), the [North Country Beagle](North_Country_Beagle "North Country Beagle"), the [Southern Hound](Southern_Hound "Southern Hound"), and possibly the [Harrier](Harrier_(dog) "Harrier (dog)").

Beagles have been depicted in popular culture since [Elizabethan](Elizabethan_era "Elizabethan era") times in literature and paintings and more recently in film, television, and comic books.

In Britain, both of these strains were then crossed with [Greyhounds](Greyhound "Greyhound") to give them speed and stamina for deer hunting.[[2]](Beagle#cite_note-2) Beagles are similar to the [Harrier](Harrier_(dog) "Harrier (dog)") and the extinct [Southern Hound](Southern_Hound "Southern Hound"), though they are smaller and slower.[[1]](Beagle#cite_note-Y110-1)

From medieval times, *beagle* was used as a generic description for the smaller hounds, though these dogs differed considerably from the modern breed. The **Bulldog** is a British [breed](Dog_breed "Dog breed") of dog of [mastiff](Mastiff "Mastiff") type. It may also be known as the **English Bulldog** or **British Bulldog**. It is a medium-sized, muscular dog of around 40–55 lb (18–25 kg). They have large heads with thick folds of skin around the face and shoulders, and a relatively flat face with a protruding lower jaw. The breed has significant health issues as a consequence of breeding for its distinctive appearance, including [brachycephalia](Brachycephalic_airway_obstructive_syndrome "Brachycephalic airway obstructive syndrome"), [hip dysplasia](Hip_dysplasia_(canine) "Hip dysplasia (canine)"), heat sensitivity, and skin infections. Due to concerns about their quality of life, breeding Bulldogs is illegal in Norway and the Netherlands.

The modern Bulldog was bred as a [companion dog](Companion_dog "Companion dog") from the [Old English Bulldog](Old_English_Bulldog "Old English Bulldog"), a now-extinct breed used for [bull-baiting](Bull-baiting "Bull-baiting"), when the sport was outlawed in England under the Cruelty to Animals Act. The Bulldog Club (In England) was formed in 1878, and the Bulldog Club of America was formed in 1890. While often used as a symbol of ferocity and courage, modern Bulldogs are generally friendly, amiable dogs. Bulldogs are now commonly kept as pets; in 2013 it was in twelfth place on a list of the breeds most frequently registered worldwide.[[4]](Bulldog#cite_note-skk-4)

## History

The first reference to the word "Bulldog" is dated 1631 or 1632 in a letter by a man named Preswick Eaton where he writes: "procuer mee two good Bulldogs, and let them be sent by ye first shipp".[[5]](Bulldog#cite_note-5) In 1666, English scientist [Christopher Merret](Christopher_Merret "Christopher Merret") applied: "Canis pugnax, *a Butchers Bull or Bear Dog*", as an entry in his *[Pinax Rerum Naturalium Britannicarum](Christopher_Merret#Bibliography "Christopher Merret")*.[[6]](Bulldog#cite_note-6)

The designation "bull" was applied because of the dog's use in the sport of [bull-baiting](Bull-baiting "Bull-baiting"). This entailed the setting of dogs (after placing wagers on each dog) onto a tethered bull. The dog that grabbed the bull by the nose and pinned it to the ground would be the victor. It was common for a bull to maim or kill several dogs at such an event, either by goring, tossing, or trampling over them. Over the centuries, dogs used for bull-baiting developed the stocky bodies and massive heads and jaws that typify the breed, as well as a ferocious and savage temperament. Bull-baiting was made illegal in England by the [Cruelty to Animals Act 1835](Cruelty_to_Animals_Act_1835 "Cruelty to Animals Act 1835").[[7]](Bulldog#cite_note-7) Therefore, the [Old English Bulldog](Old_English_Bulldog "Old English Bulldog") had outlived its usefulness in England as a sporting animal and its "working" days were numbered. However, emigrants did have a use for such dogs in the New World. In mid-17th century New York, Bulldogs were used as a part of a citywide roundup effort led by Governor [Richard Nicolls](Richard_Nicolls "Richard Nicolls"). Because cornering and leading wild bulls was dangerous, Bulldogs were trained to seize a bull by its nose long enough for a rope to be secured around its neck.[[8]](Bulldog#cite_note-8)

Bulldogs as pets were continually promoted by dog dealer [Bill George](Bill_George_(dog_dealer) "Bill George (dog dealer)").[[9]](Bulldog#cite_note-9)

In 1864, a group of Bulldog breeders under R. S. Rockstro founded the first Bulldog Club. Three years after its opening the Club ceased to exist, not having organized a single show. The main achievement of the Rockstro Bulldog Club was a detailed description of the Bulldog, known as the Philo-Kuan Standard. Samuel Wickens, treasurer of the club, published this description in 1865 under the pseudonym Philo-Kuan.[[10]](Bulldog#cite_note-10)

On 4 April 1873, [The Kennel Club](The_Kennel_Club "The Kennel Club") was founded, the first dog breeding club dealing with the registration of purebred dogs and dog breeds.[[11]](Bulldog#cite_note-11) Bulldogs were included in the first volume of the Kennel Club Stud Book, which was presented at the Birmingham Show on 1 December 1874. The first English Bulldog entered into the register was a male dog named Adam (Adamo), born in 1864.[[12]](Bulldog#cite_note-12)

In March 1875, the third Bulldog Club was founded, which still exists today.[[13]](Bulldog#cite_note-13)[[14]](Bulldog#cite_note-14) Members of this club met frequently at the Blue Post pub on [Oxford Street](Oxford_Street "Oxford Street") in <London>. The founders of the club collected all available information about the breed and its best representatives and developed a new standard for the English Bulldog, which was published on 27 May 1875, the same year they held the first breed show. Since 1878, exhibitions of the club were held annually, except during the [Second World War](Second_World_War "Second World War"). On 17 May 1894, the Bulldog Club was granted the status of a corporation and since then has carried the official name "The Bulldog Club, Inc.". It is the oldest mono-breed dog kennel club in the world.[[15]](Bulldog#cite_note-15)

The Bulldog was officially recognized by the American Kennel Club in 1886.[[16]](Bulldog#cite_note-Get_to_Know_the_Bulldog-16)

In 1894 the two top Bulldogs, King Orry and Dock Leaf, competed in a contest to see which dog could walk 20 miles (32 km). King Orry was reminiscent of the original Bulldogs, lighter boned and very athletic. Dock Leaf was smaller and heavier set, more like modern Bulldogs. King Orry was declared the winner that year, finishing the 20-mile (32 km) walk while Dock Leaf collapsed and expired.[[17]](Bulldog#cite_note-17) Though today Bulldogs look tough, they cannot perform the job they were originally bred for, as they cannot withstand the rigors of running after and being thrown by a bull, and also cannot grip with such a short muzzle. Although not as physically capable as their ancestors, modern Bulldogs are much calmer and less aggressive.[[18]](Bulldog#cite_note-18)

## Description

### Appearance

Bulldogs have characteristically wide heads and shoulders along with a pronounced mandibular [prognathism](Prognathism "Prognathism"). There are generally thick folds of skin on the brow; round, black, wide-set eyes; a short muzzle with characteristic folds called a rope or nose roll above the nose; hanging skin under the neck; drooping lips and pointed teeth, and an underbite with an upturned jaw. The coat is short, flat, and sleek with colours of red, fawn, white, [brindle](Brindle "Brindle"), and [piebald](Piebald "Piebald").[[16]](Bulldog#cite_note-Get_to_Know_the_Bulldog-16) They have short tails that can either hang down straight or be tucked in a coiled "corkscrew" into a tail pocket.

In the United Kingdom, the breed standards are 55 lb (25 kg) for a male and 50 lb (23 kg) for a female.[[19]](Bulldog#cite_note-KC_breed_standard-19) In the United States, the standard calls for a smaller dog — a typical mature male weighs 50 lb (23 kg), while mature females weigh about 40 lb (18 kg).[[20]](Bulldog#cite_note-20)

### Temperament

According to the [American Kennel Club](American_Kennel_Club "American Kennel Club") (AKC), a Bulldog's disposition should be "equable and kind, resolute, and courageous (not vicious or aggressive), and demeanor should be pacifist and dignified. These attributes should be countenanced by the expression and behavior".[[21]](Bulldog#cite_note-AKC_Bulldog_Page-21)

Breeders have worked to remove aggression from the breed.[[16]](Bulldog#cite_note-Get_to_Know_the_Bulldog-16) Most have a friendly, patient, but stubborn nature. Bulldogs are recognized as excellent family pets because of their tendency to form strong bonds with children.[[16]](Bulldog#cite_note-Get_to_Know_the_Bulldog-16) Generally, Bulldogs are known for getting along well with children, other dogs, and other pets.[[22]](Bulldog#cite_note-22)[[23]](Bulldog#cite_note-23)

## Health
